analysis.one_liner: Bans landlords from using credit checks to reject or screen renters.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would bar the use of credit reports in rental decisions, has sat in the House Financial Services Committee with no action since its introduction and no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Credit Reporting Act to prohibit anyone who rents out residential housing from pulling a renter's credit report to decide whether to approve an application, set a security deposit or lease terms, or decide whether to keep a tenant. It would apply even if the renter consents to the check, with one exception: a housing provider could still receive a report when individually reconsidering a denial. In practice it would remove credit history from the tenant screening process entirely.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters with poor, thin, or damaged credit — including people recovering from medical debt, job loss, or past evictions — would gain a fairer shot at housing, since landlords could no longer reject them, charge them larger deposits, or impose worse lease terms based on a credit score. Current tenants whose credit has slipped would also be protected from non-renewal decisions based on credit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renters with poor or no credit

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits any housing provider from using a consumer report bearing on creditworthiness, credit standing, or credit capacity to evaluate a rental application, set deposit or lease terms, or decide tenant retention [S2].
The ban applies even when the applicant consents to the credit check, and covers both prospective and current housing providers [S2].
It creates one exception: a report may still be provided to a housing provider during an individualized 'reconsideration of denial' of a rejected application [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Landlords and property managers would lose credit history as a screening tool and would bear more risk of renting to tenants they cannot pre-verify for payment history. Tenant screening companies and the three major credit bureaus would lose the rental screening business, a steady source of report fees. Some landlords might respond by raising deposits or rents across the board to cover added risk.

drawbacks.text: Landlords lose a widely used tool for predicting whether a tenant will pay rent; the bill offers no substitute standard, so some may offset the added risk by raising security deposits or rents for all applicants [S2].

The bill still permits credit checks in every other lending context, so a renter's credit history would matter for a mortgage but not for renting — a distinction critics argue can push harder-to-screen risk onto smaller landlords who have less cushion to absorb it [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For renters, this removes a barrier that often has little to do with whether someone will pay rent — credit scores are dragged down by medical debt and other obligations unrelated to tenancy. The real cost falls on landlords, who would have to screen on other grounds (income, references, rental history) and absorb more uncertainty, and some of that cost may be passed into deposits or rents. The bill is blunt: it bans credit checks outright rather than regulating how they are used, which trades precision for simplicity.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote since July 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Maxwell Frost introduced the bill on July 14, 2025 [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, and the action history shows no further action [S4].
No other member has signed on as a cosponsor [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has happened yet, so no one has won or lost materially. Landlords, tenant screening companies, and credit bureaus are better off so far simply because the ban has not advanced, while renters with bad credit are no better off than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Screening firms and landlords, so far

for.name: Rep. Maxwell Frost
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban credit checks in tenant screening.

against.name: French Hill
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup since its referral.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and it sits in a committee controlled by Republicans.

industries.note: Their core product — credit-based background reports on rental applicants — would be banned for its main use, eliminating most of the tenant screening market. Their fees are paid by applicants and landlords at the point of every rental application.
They would lose a high-volume stream of report sales to landlords and screening services, which also builds their files on renters. Renters currently pay application fees that fund these reports.

They lose credit history as a screening tool and face more uncertainty about tenant payment, which some may offset with higher deposits or rents. Their interest in keeping the screening tool runs against renters with damaged credit.

analysis.trajectory: With one sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no committee action in months, the bill is on the standard path for most House bills: it will likely die in the Financial Services Committee when this Congress ends in January 2027 unless it attracts cosponsors and a hearing.
